transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-04-23 11:00 AM PT (recorded)
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Evan Brooks (Redwood SE), Marta Lopez (CatalystHealth Eng Mgr), Ravi Patel (CatalystHealth Platform Eng), Susan Moore (CatalystHealth Security)

Summary: quick sync on the private pilot's week 3 results; focus on routing fallbacks, observed latency spikes, and a plan for the next canary with KV/prefix caching enabled. Action items and network diagram updates agreed.

Topics covered:
- Canary results and latency breakdown
- Routing: primary VPC private endpoints vs fallback to hosted API
- Firewall/NAT throughput and packet drops
- TLS certs and HSM/KMS for private keys in on-prem package
- Next canary: KV cache + adjusted batching, rollback criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: okay, good morning everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call - alex from redwood here.
[00:12] Marta Lopez: hi all, Marta here.
[00:15] Ravi Patel: ravi on platform.
[00:18] Susan Moore: susan, security.
[00:22] Evan Brooks: Evan from redwood infra.

[00:30] Alex Kim: great. so last week we flipped the pilot to the private endpoint in your VPC and ran two 1-hour canaries, one small burst and one sustained for thirty minutes. overall throughput looked good but you all flagged intermittent p99 spikes around 100 to 250 ms above baseline, is that right, Marta?
[00:48] Marta Lopez: yeah that sounds right — mostly around the 09:15 and 09:40 windows in the logs, we saw spikes and a couple of request timeouts. the thing we noticed was the spikes correlated with large batched requests from the crank-monitor service.
[01:05] Evan Brooks: just to add, our traces show those spikes were almost exclusively on the first token after a model swap — looks like KV cache misses plus a cold kv look up. could be network serialization too, borderline rtt.
[01:24] Ravi Patel: we did see our NAT gateway pushing toward the documented throughput, there were a handful of 503 from the gateway at peak. not sure if that coincides exactly but it's suspicious.
[01:37] Susan Moore: and sec, from our side, we saw no auth failures, SAML flows were fine. but we do want to confirm key storage for the on-prem package — we can't have raw keys on disk, we need HSM or KMS integration.

[01:55] Alex Kim: good call — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM via the key provider integration. Evan can share the current encryption-at-rest architecture snippet. that's on the action items.

[02:12] Evan Brooks: yeah i'll send the diagram. on the latency, two hypotheses: 1) kv cache misses — we weren't using the prefix cache for the canary, 2) NAT/backpressure on your edge. when both happen together you get the compound spike.
[02:36] Marta Lopez: can you explain prefix cache again? i thought the runtime did continuous batching and cached the kv for all active sessions.
[02:47] Evan Brooks: sure, prefix or kv cache here refers to the local per-inference-node kv cache of transformer key-values. when a session is hot, we keep the KV in memory to avoid reloading the model's past tokens. if your request routing mixes nodes, you can miss the cache. in a VPC setup with multiple nodes behind a load balancer, stickiness or routing affinity matters.
[03:12] Ravi Patel: so is the recommendation to enable session affinity on our LB? we run a multiaz NLB with ip target groups.
[03:21] Evan Brooks: affinity helps. we also ship a lightweight shared cache option (redis-backed) for cross-node hits but that trades off latency for network hop. depending on qps and size of context, redis can still be net positive.
[03:36] Alex Kim: one more routing option is to allow fallback to Redwood hosted for the tail if the private path is congested. that avoids timeouts but changes the data flow and you'd want that on only for non-sensitive payloads.
[03:52] Susan Moore: fallback to hosted is a hard sell for us — patient PHI flows must stay private. we could do fallback for non-PII analytic requests though.
[04:05] Marta Lopez: correct, we can tag requests. most of the heavy batched ones are telemetry and non-PII so maybe those can use fallback. we need a clear policy.

[04:20] Alex Kim: under review. Evan, any quick numbers from the canary? p50/p95/p99?
[04:27] Evan Brooks: p50 ~ 48ms, p95 ~ 180ms, p99 ~ 620ms during the sustained window. with KV-cache enabled in a local run we saw p99 drop to ~260ms in our bench. but that was single AZ and a smaller qps.
[04:46] Ravi Patel: so we have a dual issue: our NAT and load balancer config causing occasional 503/502, and cache misses causing higher server-side time. both add up.
[04:56] Marta Lopez: yes. and we also have some packet drops at the peering/router level during peak. will need infra to look at BGP or internal MTU mismatches.

[05:10] Alex Kim: action item: we'll send a trimmed network diagram showing the private endpoints, expected IP ranges, and suggested firewall rules. that should make the infra ticket easier.
[05:19] Susan Moore: also need the SOC2 / audit log mapping — where archived request logs will live with retention controls.
[05:26] Alex Kim: we have that in the security pack; i'll attach the relevant page to the follow-up.

[05:35] Evan Brooks: for the next canary i'd propose: enable local KV cache, add redis-shared cache fallback, set LB session affinity for a subset of nodes, and run a 30-minute sustained with your real traffic pattern. if NAT saturates we'll also simulate failure to validate fallback thresholds.
[05:58] Ravi Patel: okay simulate failover test is important. we need to know exact thresholds when Redwood will route to hosted fallback or return error. what are typical cutoff rules?
[06:09] Alex Kim: currently the pilot default is: if request latency > 5s or backend error rate > 2% for 1 minute, we can route to a configured fallback endpoint. that's configurable per-route.
[06:24] Marta Lopez: can we lower the latency cutoff for certain routes? we need stricter thresholds for user-facing paths and laxer for telemetry.
[06:31] Evan Brooks: yes per-route SLOs are supported. you can set a failover policy per API key or route. we'll share examples.

[06:44] Susan Moore: one more security question: how are audit logs correlated to our internal ids? we need to see request_id -> user_id mapping.
[06:52] Evan Brooks: we can forward structured logs to your splunk or cloud logging; we include request_id, route, model, and you can opt-in user_id pseudonymization. the logs are encrypted in transit and at rest when using KMS.
[07:08] Alex Kim: quick note — on HSM integration, we onboarded a customer last month using AWS CloudHSM and a PKCS#11 interface. if you have an on-prem HSM we can integrate but it'll need ops-level access and a short validation window.
[07:26] Ravi Patel: we'll check with security.

[07:32] Marta Lopez: back to performance - what's the recommended KV size? our average context keeps 2.5k tokens.
[07:40] Evan Brooks: for 2.5k typical KV memory per session is about 20-30MB depending on model and quantization. with 200 concurrent sessions you'd want around 6GB headroom per node. we can send a sizing sheet.
[07:58] Alex Kim: Evan, please.
[08:01] Evan Brooks: will do.

[08:07] Marta Lopez: regarding the canary, we also saw model variant swaps — someone triggered a rollout and the node swapped to 8-bit quantized variant and that caused a brief flurry of cache reloads. is there a way to lock model variant during a canary?
[08:22] Alex Kim: yes you can pin model versions per-route. during canary we usually pin the model and disable automatic rollback to avoid that noise. looks like that wasn't pinned.
[08:33] Ravi Patel: hmm that might explain a chunk of the spike. i'll follow up with the release team.

[08:40] Evan Brooks: ok, so immediate fixes for next run: 1) pin model version, 2) enable local KV cache, 3) enable LB session affinity for the canary subset, 4) monitor NAT egress and simulate failover.
[08:55] Alex Kim: sounds good. any blockers from security on our end Susan?
[09:01] Susan Moore: we need the KMS/HSM design doc and the audit log retention plan. also clarify where backups live and who can decrypt.
[09:09] Alex Kim: we'll share the security pack page and call out the KMS integration steps.

[09:16] Marta Lopez: timeline — can we run the next canary on Friday? that's when our traffic replicates production patterns.
[09:23] Evan Brooks: friday works for us, ideally early morning PT. i'll schedule the run and send an invite.
[09:29] Ravi Patel: infra team could be available to watch NAT metrics.

[09:33] Alex Kim: recap of next steps: Alex will send network diagram + security pages; Evan will run a 30-minute canary with KV/cache and share p50/p95/p99; Ravi will provide NAT throughput numbers; Marta will pin the model version for the canary.
[09:49] Marta Lopez: yep.
[09:51] Susan Moore: fine.

[09:56] Alex Kim: last thing — on rollback criteria, we'll keep the default but we'll also export the exact policy we plan to use for the canary.
[10:04] Evan Brooks: and i'll include a snippet showing how to enable redis-shared cache if you want cross-node hits.
[10:12] Alex Kim: perfect. thanks everyone, i'll follow up with the artifacts.
[10:16] Marta Lopez: thanks all.
[10:18] Ravi Patel: thanks.
[10:20] Susan Moore: bye.

End of transcript.
